prompt: Which part of Airflow works out that a task is due and hands it to a worker?
hint: It is the part that has to be awake at three in the morning.

choices.text: The web server, where the runs are drawn
choices.why: The web server shows runs and lets people clear a task; it starts nothing on its own.

choices.text: The scheduler
choices.why: Right. It reads the DAGs and the metadata database and queues what is due.

choices.text: The metadata database, which holds every run
choices.why: It holds the state the scheduler reads; it decides nothing.

choices.text: The Glue job itself, when its start time arrives
choices.why: A Glue job has no clock of its own here; something has to start it, and that is what Airflow is for.

prompt: Match each part of Airflow to what it does.
hint: Five parts, four of them here.

pairs.right: where a failed task is cleared to run again
the state of every DAG run and task instance
run the tasks taken from a queue
the Python files, in a bucket on MWAA

right_distractors: the Spark code of the Glue job

prompt: The DAG's run that starts at 03:00 on 16 October 2026 begins. What does `{{ ds }}` hold in its tasks?
hint: A run covers an interval, and it is named after the interval.

choices.text: `2026-10-16`, the day the run starts
choices.why: That is when it runs; the interval it covers is the day before.

choices.text: `2026-10-01`, the `start_date` of the DAG
choices.why: The start date is where the schedule begins, not the date of each run.

choices.text: The clock time at which the task happened to start
choices.why: A task that starts late or is re-run still gets its interval's date; that is the point of it.
Right: the run at three on the 16th covers the 15th, the partition the job should read.

prompt: Somebody copies the DAG with `catchup=True` and uploads it on 16 October; its `start_date` is 1 October. What does Airflow do?
hint: Catch-up is a backfill that nobody asked for.

choices.text: Runs the pipeline once for every night since 1 October
choices.why: Right: fifteen runs, each with its own `ds`, each starting two Glue jobs. Useful on purpose, expensive by accident.

choices.text: Runs tonight's interval and nothing earlier
choices.why: That is what `catchup=False` does.

choices.text: Refuses the file because its start date is in the past
choices.why: A past start date is ordinary; it is what catch-up counts from.

choices.text: Runs the night of 1 October and waits for a person to run the rest
choices.why: Catch-up schedules every missed interval on its own.

prompt: Why does MWAA refuse a DAG bucket that has no versioning?
hint: What does the environment record about each file?

choices.text: Versioning lets a DAG file be edited in place
choices.why: No S3 object is edited in place, versioned or not; lesson 1 showed an upload replacing it whole.

choices.text: The web server reads DAGs over a public URL that needs it
choices.why: MWAA also requires the bucket to block public access.

choices.text: It records which version of each file it loaded
choices.why: Right, and a bucket without versions cannot answer that.

choices.text: Versioned buckets are cheaper to read from
choices.why: Versioning keeps more bytes, and costs more if anything.

prompt: `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL` is `http://localhost:4567`, and `aws mwaa list-environments` cannot connect to `http://api.localhost:4567/environments`. Where did `api.` come from?
hint: The `--debug` output named it.

choices.text: moto redirected the request to a subdomain of its own
choices.why: The request never reached moto; the command line could not connect.

choices.text: The MWAA API, which puts a host prefix before the host
choices.why: Right: `host_prefix` `api.`, which the command line adds whatever the endpoint is, even an IP address.

choices.text: A typing mistake in the lab's environment variables
choices.why: Every other service in the lab uses the same variable and reaches `localhost`.

choices.text: MWAA demands HTTPS, so the command line rewrote the address
choices.why: The address it tried is still `http://`.

prompt: On a student's machine whose resolver answers names under `.localhost`, the same command gets a `500` instead of a connection error. What should the student conclude?
hint: Which program answered, and what does it have?

choices.text: An environment exists in moto, and it is broken
choices.why: There is no MWAA in moto 5.2.3 to hold one.

choices.text: Their moto has part of MWAA that the course's does not
choices.why: Both are 5.2.3; asked directly, moto answers `404` for the path.

choices.text: The request reached moto, and moto has no MWAA at all
choices.why: Right. A different road to the same answer.

choices.text: `create-environment` will now work, since the name resolves
choices.why: Resolving the name only lets the request reach a server with nothing behind that path.

prompt: Which of these really happened in this lesson's lab? Choose all that apply.
hint: Storing is not running.

choices.text: The DAG file was stored in a versioned bucket
choices.why: Yes; S3 in moto is faithful.

choices.text: The state machine's definition was stored as written
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: A cron schedule was stored with its timezone
choices.why: Yes; `get-schedule` returned it.

choices.text: The scheduler picked the DAG up from the bucket
choices.why: There is no Airflow and no MWAA in the lab.

choices.text: The state machine started the Glue job `load-orders`
choices.why: Glue answered that no such job exists.

prompt: A small environment costs 0.84249 USD an hour. What does it cost for a 30-day month of 720 hours, in USD to two decimals, with no extra workers?
hint: It is billed every hour, working or not.

prompt: The small environment is priced at 0.84249 an hour, yet the section says it costs 10.25 USD per hour of work. Where does the difference come from?
hint: Divide the month by the hours the pipeline works.

choices.text: 615.02 a month, spread over 60 hours of work
choices.why: Right: 670 of the 730 hours are paid for waiting.

choices.text: The Glue DPUs of the two jobs are included in it
choices.why: Glue is billed on its own, on top.

choices.text: Extra workers are charged at 10.25 an hour while busy
choices.why: A small extra worker is 0.09456 an hour.

choices.text: MWAA bills a minimum of twelve hours for each DAG run
choices.why: MWAA bills the environment by the hour, not the runs.

prompt: Quitanda will run no pipeline for three weeks. What can it do to stop paying for its MWAA environment meanwhile?
hint: There is no stopped state.

choices.text: Stop the environment and start it again afterwards
choices.why: An environment has no stopped state.

choices.text: Set the extra workers to zero
choices.why: That removes the 0.09456 lines; the environment's own hourly price stays.

choices.text: Delete it, losing its run history
choices.why: Right. The DAGs survive in the bucket; the record of past runs does not.

choices.text: Move it to a smaller class for the three weeks
choices.why: A smaller class is still billed every hour, and small is already the smallest of the sheet.

prompt: Forty DAGs already share one small environment comfortably. Another team adds one more DAG. What does it add to the environment's bill?
hint: What is the environment billed for?

choices.text: A forty-first share: 615.02 ÷ 41
choices.why: That is the average after; the total does not grow by a share.

choices.text: Another 615.02, since each team needs its own environment
choices.why: Teams can share an environment; that sharing is what makes MWAA cheap per pipeline.

choices.text: Close to nothing, unless it needs more workers
choices.why: Right. The environment is paid for waiting; one more DAG waits in the same hours.

choices.text: 15.38, the price per DAG the section computed
choices.why: That is an average over forty, not what one more adds.

prompt: What in the state machine plays the part that `{{ ds }}` played in the DAG?
hint: What does a state machine know about intervals?

choices.text: `$.ds`, which Step Functions fills in for each execution
choices.why: Step Functions fills in nothing of the sort; `$.` reads the input it was given.

choices.text: The `.sync` suffix on the resource
choices.why: That makes the state wait for the job; it carries no date.

choices.text: The `Retry` block of each state
choices.why: That replaces `retries=2`, not the date.

choices.text: Nothing: it gets a timestamp, and the job works out "yesterday"
choices.why: Right, and with no intervals there is no backfill either.

prompt: In the lab, `describe-execution` says `RUNNING` and `get-execution-history` ends in `ExecutionSucceeded`, through `Pass` states. Which is telling the truth?
hint: Look for a `Pass` state in `nightly.json`.

choices.text: The history: the execution succeeded quickly
choices.why: There is no `Pass` state in the definition, and the Glue job was never started.

choices.text: Neither: moto executes nothing
choices.why: Right. The status never moves, and the history is a fixed sample.

choices.text: The status: the Glue job is still running
choices.why: Glue said the job does not exist.

choices.text: Both, one after the other
choices.why: The status was read after the history was written and still said `RUNNING`.

prompt: A `Task` state whose resource is `arn:aws:states:::glue:startJobRun` with the suffix ___ added waits for the Glue job to finish before moving on.
hint: Without it, the state moves on as soon as the job has started.

prompt: Which of these does EventBridge Scheduler accept for 03:00 every day?
hint: AWS's cron has six fields and a question mark.

choices.why: Five fields is Unix cron; AWS refuses it, though moto stored it.
Minutes come first: that is 00:03.
Right: minute 0, hour 3, any day of the month, every month, any day of the week, every year.
A rate is an interval such as `rate(1 day)`, and it has no time of day.

prompt: The schedule `cron(0 3 * * ? *)` is created without `--schedule-expression-timezone`. When does it fire, in São Paulo time?
hint: Without a timezone, the expression is read in UTC.

choices.text: At 03:00, since the region is sa-east-1
choices.why: The region does not set the timezone of an expression.

choices.text: At 06:00, three hours later
choices.why: That is the UTC time of a schedule set to 03:00 São Paulo, the other way round.

choices.text: At midnight
choices.why: Right: 03:00 UTC is 00:00 in São Paulo.

choices.text: It is refused until a timezone is given
choices.why: The timezone is optional, which is why the mistake is easy.

prompt: One night Scheduler fires late and the execution starts at 03:40. The job computes "yesterday" from `<aws.scheduler.scheduled-time>`. Which day does it process?
hint: Which time does that attribute carry?

choices.text: The day before the night it was due to run
choices.why: Right. The attribute is the time the run was due, not when it started, so a late start changes nothing.

choices.text: Today, because 03:40 is after the schedule
choices.why: The job never sees 03:40; it sees the scheduled time.

choices.text: No day: a late execution gets an empty input
choices.why: Scheduler fills the attribute on every invocation, late or not.

choices.text: Two days back, since the delay pushed it past a boundary
choices.why: Forty minutes crosses no day boundary, and the time used is the scheduled one anyway.

prompt: Quitanda has two pipelines today. In a year it expects thirty-five DAGs from four teams, and frequent re-runs of past days. What plan fits?
hint: Pay for waiting when there is enough to wait for.

choices.text: MWAA now, since it will be needed in a year and moving later is work
choices.why: A year of 615.02 a month for two pipelines, about 7,380, buys nothing the alternative lacks today.

choices.text: Step Functions now, each step a dated Glue job; MWAA when the DAGs come
choices.why: Right. The jobs stay when the orchestrator changes, which keeps the move cheap.

choices.text: MWAA now, deleted every morning and created again every night
choices.why: Each deletion loses the run history, which is what backfills and re-runs depend on.

choices.text: Step Functions for good, with every re-run of a past day started by hand
choices.why: Frequent re-runs of past days by four teams is the case Airflow's intervals exist for.
